intro: In the winter of 1811 the ground under the Mississippi Valley shook so hard the river ran backward for a while. In April 2024 the sky over Carbondale went dark at two in the afternoon, exactly when astronomers said it would. Every day, millions of people in northern Illinois drink water pumped from Lake Michigan. These three things sound unrelated. They are all the same subject: Earth as a system, and what people can learn from it and do to it.

This unit follows the rock, the water, the air and the sky. You will see how plates move and why Illinois has earthquakes but no volcanoes, how the sun and gravity push water through its endless cycle, and why Illinois weather changes so fast. You will read the rock layers and fossils under the state as a calendar of billions of years, and learn why the moon changes shape and eclipses come when they do.

Then the unit turns to people. Minerals, fresh water and energy are spread unevenly, and taking them changes the land, water and air. You will look at the measurements that show Earth is warming, at what caused it, and at how communities are learning to cut their impact and check whether it worked. By the end you should be able to explain a phenomenon, point to the evidence, and say what is known and what is still uncertain.
bigQuestion: How do Earth's systems work together, and how can evidence guide what people do with the planet?

timeline.t: Galileo publishes what his telescope showed: moons circling Jupiter and mountains on the moon.
Nicolas Steno states that in layered rock, the lower layers formed first.
Isaac Newton publishes the law of gravity that explains orbits, tides and falling apples alike.
James Hutton argues that Earth is immensely old, worn down and rebuilt in endless cycles.
The New Madrid earthquakes shake the Mississippi Valley and the southern tip of Illinois.
John Tyndall measures that carbon dioxide and water vapor trap heat radiation.
Chicago reverses the Chicago River to keep sewage out of its Lake Michigan drinking water.
Alfred Wegener proposes that the continents were once joined and have drifted apart.
Charles Keeling begins measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa; it has risen every year since.
Ocean-floor mapping reveals sea-floor spreading, and plate tectonics is accepted.
U.S. clean air and clean water laws follow the tracing of pollution to its sources.
A total solar eclipse crosses Carbondale, Illinois, predicted to the second.

words.d: the never-ending set of changes that turn rock from one kind into another
the idea that Earth's outer shell is broken into plates that move and shape the surface
a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock have moved
the movement of water between air, land and sea, driven by the sun and gravity
the boundary where two different air masses meet
the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years
the imaginary line through Earth's center that it spins around; its tilt causes seasons
when the sun, Earth and moon line up so that one blocks light from reaching another

test.q: Which rock forms from sediment pressed and cemented in layers?
test.why: Limestone is sedimentary, formed from shell and mud on ancient sea floors.

test.q: Where is new ocean crust made?
choices: At divergent boundaries such as mid-ocean ridges
test.why: Plates pull apart at ridges and magma rises to make new crust.

test.q: What does the New Madrid seismic zone show about earthquakes?
choices: They happen only at plate edges
Big ones can happen on old faults in the middle of a plate
test.why: New Madrid is far from any plate edge, yet it produced huge quakes in 1811 and 1812.

test.q: Which two things drive the water cycle?
test.why: The sun lifts water by evaporation and gravity brings it down and moves it across land.

test.q: Roughly what fraction of Earth's water is salty ocean?
test.why: About 97 percent is ocean; only about 2.5 percent is fresh.

test.q: Why does Illinois get such sudden weather changes?
choices: Cold dry air from Canada and warm wet air from the Gulf meet there with no mountains in the way
It is at a high elevation
test.why: Illinois sits where very different air masses collide, and their fronts bring fast changes.

test.q: Which is a statement about climate rather than weather?
choices: Southern Illinois has a longer growing season than the north
A cold front is passing tonight
test.why: Climate is the long-term pattern; the growing season is a multi-year average.

test.q: Why is it hotter in Illinois in July than in January?
choices: Earth is closer to the sun in July
The Northern Hemisphere leans toward the sun in July, so sunlight is more direct and days are longer
The sun burns hotter in summer
The moon blocks sunlight in winter
test.why: Earth's tilt, not distance, causes the seasons; Earth is actually closest to the sun in January.

test.q: A solar eclipse can happen only at which phase?
test.why: The moon must lie between Earth and the sun, which is the new moon position.

test.q: Why do we not have a solar eclipse every month?
choices: The moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the sun
test.why: The roughly 5-degree tilt of the moon's orbit means alignment happens only a few times a year.

test.q: If you look at a star 100 light-years away, you see light that left it
test.why: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, so the light is 100 years old.

test.q: In undisturbed rock layers, which layer is the youngest?
choices: The one with the most fossils
test.why: Superposition: new sediment settles on top, so the top layer formed last.

test.q: How do scientists know Earth is about 4.5 billion years old?
choices: By radiometric dating of the oldest rocks and meteorites
test.why: Radioactive decay in the oldest rocks and meteorites gives ages near 4.5 billion years by several methods.

test.q: What did Keeling's Mauna Loa measurements show?
choices: Carbon dioxide in the air has risen every year since 1958
test.why: The record shows a steady, accelerating rise from about 315 to more than 420 parts per million.

test.q: What does 'monitoring' add to a plan to reduce human impact?
choices: It replaces the need for action
It shows whether the plan actually worked
test.why: Measuring afterward is the only way to know whether an impact was reduced.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is Illinois a safe place to live when it comes to natural hazards? Use evidence from this unit on earthquakes, tornadoes, floods and climate to support your claim, and explain how people can reduce the risk.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: safe, not safe, or safe if certain things are done.
Use at least three pieces of evidence, such as the New Madrid zone, tornado forecasting, floodplain maps or the Great Lakes water supply.
Explain the reasoning: why does each piece of evidence support your claim?
Address the other side: what would someone who disagrees point to, and how do you answer?
End with one action a community could take and how it would know if the action worked.
